utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. As you see, the proceedings have been delayed due to technical difficulties. Thanks to the diligent endeavour of the ITSS people, I'm very pleased to -- to restart right now. Okay. Mr. Karadzic, please continue. The common LiveNote is working, while personal LiveNote doesn't seem to be working at the moment, but let's continue in the meantime. Yes. I was told that in order to see the personal LiveNote, you need to restart the computer.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Excellencies. Good morning, everyone. [In English] Did you get me -- no. Good morning, I said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yesterday, we discussed the situation in Kotor Varos as an intro into what I want to show you concerning directive number 4, but before that I want to show you one more document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] D1324, please, in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While we're waiting, Mr. Butler, do you believe me if I say that after what happened in Kotor Varos -- no, that's not the right document. D1324. D12 -- 1324. Not 1234 but 1324. Do you take my word for it that many traumatic events occurred for both sides? There was a lot of revenge, the civilians had gone, the combat unit remained, and then fierce fighting developed. There were personal settlement of accounts, killings, revenge, et cetera. I don't know if you dealt with it yourself, but would you believe me if I say that happened?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot speak specifically to Kotor Varos, but clearly the description of the situation that you've described would also easily fit the territory of Eastern Bosnia in 1992 through 1995 as well. So I would agree with your general premise, although like I said, I cannot comment on what did or did not happen in Kotor Varos.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Look at item 2, please, second paragraph. Captain Zupljanin informed the War Presidency of a report that the soldiers from Vecici have abandoned the village. The population also left and is in Hadzirica Potok. And now the populous is gone, and they went further on towards Central Bosnia, and they passed through safely. Very well. Let's look at directive number 4 now, P976. You are familiar with it; right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Excuse me. I may be missing it. Does this document say that they passed through safely? I'm --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, it's not written there, but it's written that both left but going in two different directions. The civilians went to Hadzirica Potok.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. I just -- from the record and the transcript it looked as though that was written on the document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 976 is the number, I believe. P976.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. In answer to your question, I am familiar with this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we now look at item 6 relating to the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Page 5 in English.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Item (d) says the Drina Corps. Now, I'd like to ask you this: Do you recall, and I believe I asked you the same thing yesterday, how many requests were made through Morillon and in other ways for civilians to be moved from the area of combat operations in Eastern Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, my answer from yesterday is that I am aware that on a number of occasions there were requests made and that the UN did seek to in Eastern Bosnia facilitate the movement of civilians out of active combat areas. I do not recall a number of those requests. However, I believe that they are well laid out in the United Nations report relating to the fall of Srebrenica, and so those details are available in that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Here in directive 4 it is written somewhere, but I can't locate it now because I don't have hard copy --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I see the next page in Serbian. "Mladic requested." I beg your indulgence for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. Under (d) it says -- I'll be reading in English because I've lost the Serbian page. "[In English] First offered the disarming of able-bodied and armed men, and if they refuse, destroy them. Then unblock the Milici-Konjevic Polje-Zvornik road," and so on and so on. [Interpretation] It seems to have been revised because earlier it sounded -- asking them to surrender, but it's really to disarm them. I want to ask you -- I don't know if it's the same thing in English as in Serbian. If you were going somewhere, would there be a difference if I said your wife would be going with you and that your wife would be -- that you would be going with your wife? Does it make a difference in English? Who leads in one case and who leads in the alternative?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure I can help you with that particular transliteration on my experience. I've been married for 31 years and I've never been in charge, so in all scenarios, I'm going wherever my wife's going.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. It's much the same in my case, but let's say that it's going with your brother. If we say Dr. Butler would be going with his brother as opposed to Mr. Butler's brother would be going with him, who is leading and who is following?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I don't know whether it's an issue of linguistics with respect to directive 4, but, I mean, to raise the issue -- I mean, the issue as it is written is whether or not the military is the object of attack and that as the military withdraws, the civilians attempt to go with them or whether the civilian population itself is one of the objects of attack, presumably with the military. And therein lies the issue of the language in this particular paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: However, it is a very essential issue. I'll show you. When it says, "and forced them with the Muslim population to leave Birac," [In English] What if I would change the order or the sequence of the words and say, "and forced them to leave with the Muslim population" as it is in original?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the, sir, the version that I'm looking at in English says as follows, and I'll start with the clause in question: "Inflict the heaviest possible losses on them and force them with the Muslim population to leave Birac, Zepa, and Gorazde areas." This is what it says on the English language translation that I'm looking at.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. But let's look now at this. Does the sense change if we put the word "leave" before "the population," "and forced them to leave with the Muslim population"?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not wishing to quibble over linguistics on this issue, for me as a military analyst, the definition of what this meant to the military commanders on the ground would be best reflected by how the campaign was conducted by those military officers within the Drina Corps and within the various brigades that were conducting them. And it is my position, having looked at that and looked at how that particular campaign was conducted, I conclude that at least in part the civilian population, their structures, and their towns and villages were objects of attack. So attacking the civilians were not a by-product or a collateral impact of the military operations. Moving the civilian population more or less permanently from the region was a military goal.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: However, Dr. Butler, look at this analogy. This is two weeks after the incident in Vecici. Two weeks later after an identical incident, the civilians want to go, the army wants to stay. Mladic orders here the army to follow the civilians, not the civilians to follow the army. So it's not the army leading the civilians. It is -- the civilians who want to go anyway are to take the troops with them, because a similar dispute occurred in Kotor Varos in the case of Vecici. Do you see that one follows from the other?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: First, sir, while I appreciate the sentiment, I am not a doctor or professor. Second, in light of the geographic distance and the fact that one incident is occurring in the zone of the Krajina corps and one is -- and one operation or planned series of operations is occurring in the Drina Corps, I don't believe that there's a causal link between the two. Again, it may reflect your particular wish that this is how a campaign may be conducted. However, in the operative document it is not drafted or written that way, and if one were to examine the conduct of the campaign, it is my belief that it was not fought that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I appreciate your saying that it's your opinion, but do you agree that two weeks earlier, in the case of Vecici, when there was a dilemma whether only civilians should go while the army should surrender, wasn't Mladic involved in the same dispute two weeks earlier opposing my instructions initially? Does Mladic conflate these two events? He had an experience with it two weeks earlier, and now he's making a slightly different order after the traumatic experience in Kotor Varos. It's the same player in both cases, Mladic.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I mean, I -- I agree to the extent that what happened in Kotor Varos happened in Kotor Varos. My point is that in a country that is seeing significant conflict and these issues are arising up in various locations on a daily basis, to take one isolated data point or issue in time and seek to extrapolate that into a cause and effect mechanism I don't believe is a sound analytical practice. So again, it might very well be as you describe the situation. However, looking at one solitary incident that happened in another area of the country and under the control of other military forces, albeit General Mladic, and seeking to extrapolate that to other areas I don't believe is sound.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But if I tell you that if I had read this directive, which I didn't because I didn't sign it, if I had seen this directive and knowing what had happened in Kotor Varos, do you believe that I would have known what it's all about or that his colleagues in the staff understood why this order was different, that troops also had to leave, because it was not -- not done in Kotor Varos, but here it's going to be different. Mladic orders the troops to leave as well.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As -- as -- to answer the first part of your assertion, I have no way of knowing whether you read this particular directive or not. The fact that you did not sign this directive anywhere, in my opinion is not proof that you had no ability to read this directive at some juncture or even to comment on it at some juncture. It just simply means that there is no signature from you on it. Again, to the second particular issue, I don't know what you did or did not consider related to this and again how it linked up to the incident that you discuss in Kotor Varos.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. But you have no proof that I had read this directive or commented upon it; correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, sir, your assertion was that you did not read this directive because you did not sign this directive. I don't know whether that's the case or not. I have no information one way or another.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to ask you this: I have seen and I'm thankful that in the examination-in-chief you provided a few clarifications and views that follow from your knowledge of the international laws of warfare. Is it true that you are familiar with the international laws of warfare?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I would qualify my familiarity with the rules and laws of international warfare as that ironically enough, my primary knowledge of them is derived from my understanding of the SFRY rules on the application of the international laws of war and my research on that particular document as it related to the greater body of my research. As you are aware, I am not a legal professional or lawyer in that sense or academic, so I can't comment on broader issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I was waiting for the interpretation. But you were able to say yesterday that a certain type of military conduct is legal or customary, lawful; correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, in the context of how it is described in those SFRY regulations which by your decree were applicable to the army and the armed forces of the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that the party that declares war has certain obligations both to its own civilians and the civilians of the other party?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: My understanding is that all parties to a conflict, not just the party that declares war, have certain obligations inherent in the Geneva Conventions, the Additional Protocols, and whatever customary laws are in effect related to the protection of various classes of noncombatants, as well as civilian properties. I don't believe that protections raise or lower or there are different standards depending upon which party initiated an armed conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you notice which party in Bosnia-Herzegovina declared war?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As part of my research into what happened, the actual designation of who started it wasn't a relevant issue. The work that I was asked to do by the Office of the Prosecutor was to examine the military situations in various contexts, and again, frankly, you know, who was the good guys, who were the bad guys, who were the friendlies, and who were the enemies was not relevant to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Although it is not relevant, do you know the answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, sir, I don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Would you agree -- did you come across somewhere in the document to the reference that the Muslim side, on the 22nd June, 1992, declared war against Serbia, Montenegro, and the Serbian autonomous regions in Bosnia-Herzegovina, effective as of 22nd June? And to assist you, did you find in my appeals to the Muslim side to cancel the war and to terminate the war as a short-term conflict?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, sir, that may be the case with respect to declarations, but the starting point of armed conflict, at least with respect to my research, begins on 1 April 1992, with the first battles and activities that take place in the town of Bijeljina. Now, again, I can see that it's not a complete view of the entire country and conflict involving Bosnia-Herzegovina and Republika Srpska, but that was the starting point with respect to my analytical work.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. So on the 1st of March there was a ceremony, there was a wedding, and someone was killed in Sarajevo. And you don't take that event to be the beginning of the war.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, sir, given that my mandate with respect to focusing my analysis was on Eastern Bosnia, what incidents in other parts of the country that might have "triggered the war," it was just not a topic that I -- that I passed judgement on or even looked at. For me, the effective date of the start of hostilities was 1 April.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But wouldn't the beginning have been on the 25th or 26th of March when the Muslim forces killed in Bosanski Brod, they looted the possessions of entire families. But would your opinion perhaps be that if there was no resistance, then there was no war being waged?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. My answer is I don't know. What -- given that I already had a full plate with the tasks that I already had to do, and particularly given the context of my focus of study being July of 1995, what happened in 1992 in other locations outside of Eastern Bosnia was not relevant to my work. I just did not pay attention to it, and it is not an issue that I believe has any bearing on what happened in July of 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Nevertheless, given the context in Eastern Bosnia, you referred to directive number 4. You referred to events in the spring of 1993 when the Serbian side liberated Podrinje. Isn't that right? And then there were certain events in Eastern Bosnia, and so to speak it was the first half-time with respect to these events.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As you note, sir, in my report I do discuss from the historical context portion the military operations that did occur in Eastern Bosnia in 1992 and the beginning of 1993 through the establishment of the United Nations safe areas, and I agree that with the establishment of the United Nations safe areas, particularly in some regions of Eastern Bosnia, armed conflict ebbed down to a much lower level than one had seen or one had observed in November, December, of 1992, and then January through March and April of 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I still want to deal with these general issues and I'll rely on your familiarity with the events and your familiarity with our regulations. You did read the indictment, did you not, the indictment brought against me?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not believe I have read the latest version of your indictment, no, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But you have read the first and second version of that indictment, haven't you?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You have also read other indictments that relate to other cases that you testified in. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And in those other cases, you adapted your report. You adapted your report to those cases, to those accused? Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Partially. I would answer that I tailored particularly issues related to command and control, the relevant regulations, as well as the applicable rules to reflect those that were most pertinent to the rank and position of the accused during that particular case, and that was my motivation for not changing previous reports but, in fact, authoring new reports that would reflect that information more tailored for the use of the Office of the Prosecutor and, as it turned out, ultimately the Trial Chambers. So in that sense I did tailor the document to the relevant issues at hand as I understood them. I did not change issues of the reports or the factual issues in them in any way to correlate more closely to the actual language of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was this your choice or did the Prosecution request that you proceed in this way?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. I had an almost unlimited autonomy with respect to the content, the context, and what material I would or would not put in my reports. So the Prosecution, you know -- in previous discussions and as it's noted I've been -- at that time I'd been a member of the Prosecution team -- or investigative team with respect to Srebrenica since April of 1997, so I was very cognisant, obviously, of the level of command or rank of the various accused. So I already intrinsically knew in my mind what type of products I would produce that would be, again, most useful initially to the investigative teams as they were looking at these cases and then ultimately, as it turns out, for the Office of the Prosecutor to tender in the various cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As a loyal member of the Prosecution, you didn't make any efforts that might be useful to the Defence, did you?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: My mandate with respect to my military analysis was to present the situation as to what the military documents meant within the conduct -- or within the context as best that I understood them. I will tell you that obviously much of that material clearly was favourable to the Prosecution in light of the crimes that occurred. I can also tell you that information that I raised in those reports was also deemed to be beneficial to the Defence in some cases. And certainly in the case of a clarification on some issues related to testimony with General Krstic, my clarification on some issues was instrumental, I believe, in the Appellate Court reducing his sentence to some degree. So the information that I provide is the information that I provide as a result of my work. Who it benefits and under what circumstances ultimately is a decision for the relevant Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So given the huge amount of material, and you didn't use or the material available, you had to make a selection of the material that you would produce. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, and in fact, I believe I discuss as part of the forwards in the various reports that I've authored the fact that I'm not seeking to undertake a full historical accounting of all of the events in Eastern Bosnia. This is not -- you know, this is a legal forum. This is not an academic forum. I had to obviously tailor the information to reflect the issues that were under consideration by the Trial Chambers. So to the degree that I can explain that in the forwards, I did. Clearly, the Prosecution and Defence in various cases throughout the, I guess, intervening 12 years now have had numerous opportunities to add information, to raise those various issues, and my willingness to explore those new issues as they come up as necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But in the course of your work as an investigator, you became -- you came to come to certain -- you came to have certain convictions with regard to the responsibility certain individuals had and with regard to the way in which events unfolded. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I have opinions as to those. Many of those opinions are in my reports and are the basis of a number of the conclusions that I make in those reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. It seems that the Prosecution also used you for certain searches. Did you in fact participate in any of the searches that were conducted?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'd like to know the following: Given that you were an investigator and a member of the Prosecution and given that you came to have certain convictions, how did it come to pass that you became an expert witness? And by definition, an expert witness has to be neutral, unbiased.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I can tell you is that I don't invite myself to these parties. I am called, in most cases, by the Office of the Prosecutor. I am aware that issues relating to my appearance before various Trial Chambers have been litigated in prior Trial and Appellate Chambers. My position is as it's always been. I'm called by the Office of the Prosecutor as a witness, and that ultimately it will be the Trial Chamber who will accept or not accept issues that I have raised or have said or opinions that I may or may not have made or agreed with, and ultimately they will draw their own conclusions and put the weight where they see it needs to be, and in reading past judgements related to Srebrenica, it is clear that Trial Chambers do exactly that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Since you tailored and updated, I assume, your report in other cases if, for example, other documents were found, how is it that in this case where the Supreme Commander is accused and the head of state, how is it in this case you didn't produce a special report, you didn't tailor your report?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't asked. The -- I mean, I won't speak for the Office of the Prosecutor, but it appears that the previous reports that I had authored were sufficient for their needs in this particular case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That's why I asked you whether they had asked you to proceed in this way in other and earlier cases, and you said that they hadn't made such a request. You said you were autonomous. If you could act autonomously in those cases, did you feel the need to produce a special tailored report in this case, a report that would concern me, myself, and my responsibility?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there are several answers. First off, I don't publish friends of the court reports. When specifically asked by a party to do that, in most cases -- I guess in all cases, it's been the Office of the Prosecutor in various forms I've testified. If my time allows, I'm happy to undertake that, given the technical restrictions that, one, are on my time, as well as the fact that I do not have daily, immediate access to the vast archives of material that I understand have come into the possession of the ICTY since my departure here in November of 2003. So, ultimately, if the Prosecution had asked for me to draft a report, I would. Or I could, I should say. Once I'm asked to draft that report, what I am to say in it, what conclusions I draw, and what material I elect to use or not use is entirely my own.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If the Prosecution made such an admission, well, would you have responded to a Defence request to conduct such an analysis? And my question only concerns the Supreme Command.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a member of the United States government and particularly within the Department of Homeland Defence - okay - there are various governmental regulations with respect to United States government employees testifying on behalf of defendants. So the reality of that situation is that any such request would have to be cleared by various individuals within the Department of Homeland Security before I could even entertain such a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does that mean that according to the government's rules, you are not prohibited from testifying on behalf of the Defence? Is this allowed?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, sir. The rules do not specifically prohibit me. It requires that I seek the permission of various other agencies within the Department of Homeland Security who will ultimately make that decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In any event, you're aware of the fact that during the crisis there was a disagreement between us and the US government? Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a pretty broad phrase. I mean, if you're willing to be specific, I can make specific answers to that to the degree that I know them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Would you agree that the US government unreservedly supported the Muslim side even when it came to illegally providing them with arms, let alone when it was a matter of conducting negotiations and finding solutions? Wouldn't that be something you became convinced of?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware through my work here at the Tribunal and the research that I have done that various UN reports, as well as reports from the various warring parties at the time, do indicate that there was some support with respect to the supply of weapons to Bosnian Muslim military forces that were reported to have originated from the United States. I have no firsthand knowledge of that, obviously, and again, my knowledge of that is done based off of the reporting done either by the United Nations or that is incorporated in the various reports of the warring parties. So in that respect, I can't really comment further on that. I am aware of it, but I do not know the specific details, and it was not a particular topic which I looked into.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. To conclude with this issue, I'm wondering whether it would be possible for you to be unbiased in this case given your loyalty to the Prosecution and given your loyalty to the US government? Is it possible for you to make such an effort? Is it possible for you to remain unbiased?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can tell you that as a professional analyst, the issue of bias creeping into reports and analysis by any individual is an obvious concern. I am aware of that. And while I can be, as described by some people, ruthlessly analytical, I am human. I cannot escape the fact that there may be bias. Hence the purpose of cross-examination as well as the ability of the Trial Chamber to review those issues and put whatever appropriate weight they deem necessary on the information I'm providing in light of that potential bias.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us whether you went through all the documents that the Prosecution had access to? And at least in respect to Eastern Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: With respect to Eastern Bosnia, up to the end of my period of work here with the Office of the Prosecutor, in November of 1993 I had access to all material in that respect that was in the possession of the Office of the Prosecutor. It worked out convenient that way since it was my people actually having to catalogue the material. Obviously, once my time here was completed, it would no longer be possible for me to have complete access to all of the material. In light of the fact that it was recognised that I would be potentially coming back to the Tribunal in various capacities and might be asked to do additional reports, arrangements were made with the permission of the Office of the Prosecutor and the United States government that allowed for me to access the Office of the Prosecutor's document collections through the EDS system. So as I was asked to do additional research, I had access to the base material if I so elected to use it. So even in the context of the updated reports, one, the Prosecutor sent me all documents that I requested, not just the ones that they felt might be relevant, and even independent of that, I had the ability to independently search through material to be able to include any material that I believed was relevant regardless of what the Office of the Prosecutor might have thought.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So the initial selection of material was made by the Prosecution; right? And then they sent you documents that were relevant to them; right? That's what you said a moment ago, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. I did not say that the initial sort or selection was made by the Office of the Prosecutor. At the time that I was making the reports while I was here, I had sole control over all of the documents that I chose to include in my reports for whatever reason. With respect to the Main Staff Responsibility Report that I was asked to undertake in 2006, I believe, clearly I was not here at the time, but I already had a basis for much of that report from material that I had already accumulated from my previous reports. I was also sent material by the Office of the Prosecutor for potential consideration, and that's the key. They offered material for consideration. It was ultimately my decision whether to place such material in the report or not and to conclude what I thought that material meant in context of the report I was writing. What I've also said in that regard is the fact that even beyond that, I still retained a capability to independently review material myself directly via EDS at the time so I could ensure myself that I had a full, complete, or at least representative selection of all of the material that I would be potentially including in my report and drawing conclusions on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'm going to embark on a series of questions that would probably lend themselves to mere yes or no answers. Did you focus on documents that pertained to me personally, or did you make a sub-file that would pertain to my indictment?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: With respect to which report, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The reports that were a basis for your report, for your findings, everything that you came across.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The framework for that is I obviously focused on brigade-level materials for the brigade command report, corps materials for the corps, Main Staff materials for the Main Staff report, and in the original narrative document, as well as the revised narrative document, I have a broad spectrum of documents related to the entire crime base. I don't recall ever having a Dr. Karadzic file in that particular sense that one day I presumed I would be writing a report about you in your role as the Supreme Commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your work did you come across what is known as mitigating documents or potentially mitigating, and, if so, what did you do with them?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I did. As a member of the Office of the Prosecutor then and even today, I considered myself bound by the provisions of ICTY Rule 68, which deals with the disclosure to the Defence of any materials which are deemed to be potentially exculpatory for any defendant. During the military analysis phase where we were reviewing the documents, where I was writing the reports and even afterwards, there was a process in place where any document that I or any member of my review team believed could be potentially exculpatory to any defendant, that particular document would be flagged, and I would personally bring it to the attention of the senior trial attorney on any given case. I would lay out why I believed the document was exculpatory, and if additional justifications were needed, I would provide those justifications. And I believe that perhaps the best explanations of that were probably outlined in the Krstic appeal brief and judgement where issues of Rule 68 violations were raised by the Defence and the Prosecution's answers to them as well as the Court's findings. I think particularly from a military perspective, I'm highly confident that during my time here any document that we believed was potentially exculpatory was disclosed to the Defence. I'm not aware of a particular situation where I believed that a document that was potentially exculpatory wouldn't have been disclosed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. However, you did not include them in your report; right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I included the documents that were relevant to the entire crime base as well as the various issues in my report. I guess it's a question of interpretation as to what is exculpatory to whom. I would remind you that in the Popovic case, the basic Defence theories lined up between the commanders were responsible for the actions of all of their subordinates versus the security officers had taken independent charge of various forces. Documents that might be viewed as exculpatory to military commanders would not be viewed the same as exculpatory to security officers and, of course, vice versa. The material was included in the reports for all concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Perhaps my question may sound strange to you, but we do not have an adversary system in our part of the world. Our investigations are supposed to be comprehensive and two-sided, if you will. Let me ask you this now: Did you mention at least in the footnotes that there may be another explanation as well, because there is a document that is potentially exculpatory, or did you stick to what the Prosecution expected of that report?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I attempted to make my reports as balanced and reflective of the military situation and the command and control situation, as well as the legal authorities that were in place at the time, as I possibly could. Again, even in the event that such material was not incorporated in my reports, and I don't believe that I didn't do it in such a manner that I excluded material like that, Defence counsel for numerous cases have had the opportunities over the last 12 years now of raising those specific issues and those specific documents to me on the basis of my testimony here, hearing my explanations as to why they are in the report or why they are not in the report, and perhaps of more importance to the Court, what it means in context to what is occurring in Srebrenica and making their own determinations as to the document's relevancy as well as my motivations for either including the document or not including the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you have an opportunity to quote documents exactly? Did you have a service that could check whether what you were quoting in the English language was properly and accurately translated in the first place?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Just like everybody else, we used the offices of the ICTY's translation service, the CLSS, and the overwhelming majority of the documents were translated by that service. There was one or two documents because of time constraints that may have been interpreted or translated by other individuals assigned to the OTP, but again, just like everyone else, I am completely dependent upon the translations provided by CLSS for the interpretations that I make in the English language documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does that also pertain to transcripts of intercepts? Did you have an opportunity to listen to some intercepts? Did you check the transcripts, whether they were correct? Of course I don't mean you personally. I mean your services, the staff.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, sir, the intercepts to my knowledge, most of them were translated by CLSS. So that's the first question. And second, with relation to the intercepts, yes, I did have opportunities to listen to various audiotapes. Not that I could understand the language, but being a military intelligence officer, I at least have some layman's familiarity with signals intercepts to at least verify for myself that what I was listening to and that was purported to be an intercept was an intercept. And further, I actually had occasions to visit at least one of the intercept sites, examined the equipment there to satisfy myself that the Bosnian Muslim military at the time had the technical capability of collecting on the information that was purported to be by everyone an intercepted communication -- or an intercept of VRS communications.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know -- actually, I think that you showed in the examination-in-chief that you were familiar with the laws of the SFRY and thereby of Bosnia-Herzegovina and Republika Srpska as well, laws that pertain to the military and to defence; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. And the relevant portions, I believe, are incorporated in my reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Hank you. Does that also pertain to provisions of the Law on All People's Defence and social self-protection? Are you familiar with this particular wording from the period of Socialist self-management, All People's Defence and social self-protection and the law governing it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am familiar with the phrase and general concept of All People's Defence. I believe -- I mean, clearly that was the military doctrine under which many of the regulations and manuals were drafted in order to implement during various stages of an armed conflict in the former Yugoslavia. So while I do for the most part quote those actual military regulations and manuals with respect to how they apply to various military echelons and not so much going back to the -- the general principles of All People's Defence, I do have some awareness of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you also made aware of laws of other countries in the field of the military and defence in general, and in that sense, did you notice anything that might be termed as a differentia specifica as far as our laws and the military and defence are concerned?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not do a comparative study of the Law on the Army and the Law on Defence and how that may compare or contrast to laws of other countries. I did not believe that that type of analysis was necessary for understanding the events as they occurred with respect to Srebrenica in July of 1995 or necessary to understand how the military programme of command and control worked within the Army of the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: However, you will agree that that could be important for understanding the role of the president of the republic, who is at the same time the civilian head of the military; right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, understanding how the supreme leadership of the United States or Canada or Mexico, for that matter, and how it might relate to your roles and responsibilities under the law of the Republika Srpska might be interesting and perhaps even instructive in an abstract sense, but I don't believe it was relevant with respect to how command and control functioned within the armed forces of the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you notice any difference between our laws and the laws of the SFRY? We took over the laws of the SFRY, but we did change certain things. Did you notice any of these changes?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are a lot of circumstances, as you note, where there were wholesale adoptions of various blocks of law by the Republika Srpska of the former SFRY law. One comes to mind, of course, is the wholesale adoption of the RS Criminal Code or the former SFRY Criminal Code by the Republika Srpska and there were some minor deviations. Having said that, there were other laws that there were more detailed deviations on to more clearly meet the requirements of the government of the Republika Srpska. There are hundreds of these types of changes, and again, if you wish to, you know, show me a specific passage, I can hopefully be instructive there, but I don't know that I can get more specific than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, let me be more specific then. Did you notice that there was a difference between the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia and the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, or more specifically, from a doctrinary establishment and practical point of view, is there anything special in the existence of a General Staff on the one hand and a Main Staff on the other? From the point of view of the role of the head of state.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: There may well be, sir, but it was not an area that I examined. For the relevant period in July 1995, the Army of the Republika Srpska was managed by a Main Staff. My goal was to understand to the degree that I could how that staff worked. How that compared with the command and control apparatus of the Federal Army of Yugoslavia or even the Republic of Croatia, I did not believe to be relevant. The Republika Srpska Army and the Supreme Command are bound by the laws that are enacted by and in effect within the Republika Srpska. They're not bound by the laws and procedures of other states.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. However, from that point of view --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one question, Excellency, please, and then the break?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: From that point of view, did you establish whether there was a difference in terms of the relationship with the head of state if there is a Main Staff or if there is a staff of the Supreme Command? And then in that case there is a Chief of Staff, whereas in the Main Staff there is a commander. Let me remind you of this as well: You noticed that this situation with the Supreme Command staff, I wanted to deal with that in the beginning of August 1995, and I did not succeed; right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I would say in answer to your first question is that since I did not do a comparative study of how the Main Staff worked in comparison to how, for example, the federal staff worked within the Yugoslav army, the General Staff there, I can't answer that question with respect to those specific issues. I just don't know enough about the former Yugoslav General Staff to be able to answer that question. As to your second question, I am aware of issues between you and the VRS in August of 1995. They are rather complex and detailed and might -- I could answer the question now rather lengthily, or it might be more appropriate to wait after the break. It's not going to be a short answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Food for thought. In documents, did you find any elements of my dissatisfaction with the level of control that I had, and was the reason for this change in August based on that? You don't have to answer now. If you wish, you can answer after the break.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can answer quickly that, yes, I found evidence of that in the documents. Expanding as to what to the basis on that may or may not have been and all of the variables, again I would leave it up to the Court whether they wish to go into that before or after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Before we take a break and before we move away from the document which is before us, i.e., directive number 4, I'd like to deal with the translation issue the accused raised. Could we collapse the B/C/S version and zoom in to the English version. I take it this is page 5, para (d), relating to the Drina Corps. Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I don't mean to interrupt, but if my memory serves me, this -- a similar issue came up with the testimony of General Milovanovic, and I believe that the version we have in e-court is a revised translation that has already been revised once. I just wanted to alert --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether this part I'm going to raise is also dealt with. In any event, in the middle paragraph in para (d), the last part of the first sentence reads as follows: "... and force them with the Muslim population to leave the Birac Zepa, and Gorazde areas." However, as noted in the accused's question on transcript page 5, lines 6 to 9, and I think he raised this issue before as well, it seems to be his submission that the correct translation should be as follows: "... and force them to leave the Birac, Zepa, and Gorazde areas with the Muslim population." Therefore, whatever a nuance there may be, it seems prudent to clarify this issue. So therefore I ask the CLSS to file a written filing before the Chamber, paying attention to the sequence or location of the phrase "with the Muslim population."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may, Excellency, may I suggest something. Could the CLSS clarify this for us: In the spirit of the Serbian language, who does this verb "to force" refer to, the civilian population or the armed forces?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. I would ask the CLSS to take that into account as well. Then we'll take a break for half an hour as indicated. So we will resume at 10 past 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Before the break, we were dealing with the difference between the General Staff and the Main Staff -- or, rather, the General Staff with the chief at its head. How are things organised in your country? In my time, there was Colin Powell there. I don't know what the case is now, but was he a commander or the Chief of Staff?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, General Colin Powell was, I believe, the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Given all your knowledge, if we asked you to create a legal basis for the Defence for the VRS, well, is there anything that would change there? Is there anything that bothered you or that one might think bothered us, was a hindrance to us?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm not sure I understand your question, whether it's referring to -- I mean, the defence with respect to the legal defence here before the Tribunal, or are you talking about defence and army laws or -- I just am not clear as to what you're trying to get at, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I apologise. That was my mistake. When examining the documents that pertain to the war we waged, did you notice any structural weaknesses, any legal restrictions, and if you were to create a legal basis for the defence of the republic and for the army in that republic, is there anything you yourself would change within our system? I'm referring to the organisation and command and control.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, respectfully, sir, my role first as a military analyst in my own army was to be able to analyse and understand how a military system worked, particularly at an operational and tactical level for the purpose of being able to understand it and against a potential armed adversary degrade or destroy it. The various legal underpinnings of why a Department of Defence or a Ministry of Defence works, how it is inter-related with the civilian system and all of those particular functions is an area of many other people's great expertise. So again, my role here is to understand the current system as it was operating and how it was relevant, particularly in the month of July of 1995, not to examine it with respect to how it might be made better or whether I believed it was the perfect system. I mean, the fact is, I guess as underscored by the Prosecution of the conflict for three years until it was terminated in November of 1995, was, whether it was perfect or not, it was good enough to allow for the necessary interrelation between the civilian political branches of government and the armed forces in order to defend the requirements of the state.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned the operational and tactical level of command. Who was responsible for these two levels of command given the information that you came across in the documents that pertain to that issue?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the most part, the day-to-day military operations, at least with respect to the army, were under the control of the Main Staff and their subordinate formations, those being the corps of the VRS and their subordinate brigades.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you notice that our law contained provisions according to which the president of the republic can delegate operational and tactical issues to the Main Staff? And this, in fact, was done in one of the documents concerning the army's organisation and establishment.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that there is specific language to that effect in the Republika Srpska Law on the Army. I can't quote you verbatim what paragraph or article it might be, but it is incorporated in my reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So is it customary for the civilian head of the state and of an army to be involved only in strategic matters and operational tactical matters are for the army, for the Main Staff, or for the headquarters that had its own commander? Or was this an exceptional case that you came across?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe that it is exceptional in that sense. I guess I -- notwithstanding my military roots, I believe it was former President Lincoln in the United States during the Civil War who noted that war was too important to be left strictly to military commanders. War is a means to achieve political objectives through the use of force, in its simplest definition, I guess. So the military component of that, the armed forces component of how that will be prosecuted cannot be divorced from the political goals of the state as articulated by its leadership.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If everything functions as it should do.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The -- how the apparatus is set up is, of course, dictated by first the laws and then the rules and regulations that are affected to implement the laws. How they are implemented ultimately depends upon the various political and military leaders of the state. Leadership is, at the end of the day, a personal function.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you come across in our laws a provision of any kind that directs or orders the commission of crimes? Could anyone refer to such a provision as a justification for having committed a certain crime? And I think you can answer that question simply by saying yes or no.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- the answer is: I did not come across any document like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you come across any documents that provides for impunity for perpetrators of war crimes?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can tell you that within the context of the Criminal Code of then the Republika Srpska, which was, of course, adopted from the SFRY, as well as various other orders and documents, there was no legalistic provision for impunity. In fact, in the SFRY regulations relating to the application of the laws of armed conflict, as well as within the RS Criminal Code, it specifically noted that, you know, committing war crimes on orders was not a defence in that particular sense. So there's nothing codified under law or regulations that I am aware of that would allow any individual to claim immunity for acts that are clearly recognised as war crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you come across a single document, for example, from myself or from the government or other civilian structures, in which it was ordered that a crime should be committed or in which the order was not to sanction a crime that had, in fact, been committed?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sir, I guess, one, first limiting this to the documents that I have reviewed with respect to Eastern Bosnia, I would say that is an interpretational issue. For example, as I have testified before, not here, but I believe in a previous Srebrenica-related case, that looking at the language of directive 4, as I understand the English language translation of have, it is my view that that wording as written would constitute an unlawful order insomuch as the fact that it directs in part a military attack against a civilian population.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, we'll get to that perhaps later, but since you mentioned it, let me ask you the following: Are you aware of the fact that according to our Law on All People's Defence it's obligatory to evacuate the civilians from war zones regardless of whether this is what they want?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No objection, but I would like a cite to that provision, if he can give me one.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, in the law that we adopted. I wasn't going to produce that, but I just wanted to know whether Mr. Butler took this into consideration when compiling his report. Did he take into consideration the fact that it is obligatory to evacuate the civilians? And that is also the case in his country.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When there is a hurricane, evacuating the people is obligatory. Orders are then issued to that effect. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, maybe to get to the first point, while it may be the case, I am not aware of a decree that the former SFRY Laws on All People's Defence were adopted and incorporated as the Republika Srpska Law on All People's Defence. Maybe it was redesignated as the RS Law on Defence and they left out the "All People," but I don't know that to be the case. So I don't know that it was your law, first of all. And second, as I've testified previously, I don't know the whole Law of All People's Defence and all of its underpinnings, so again, if you wish to show me that and I can comment on it, I can, but I'm not familiar with the provision that you're talking about under law.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If we have time, I'll show you the relevant document. But are you aware of the fact that as of the 11th of April, 1992, up until the 1st of October, 1992, well, during that period, in fact, we signed a number of agreements under the auspices of the UNHCR, under the auspices of Lord Carrington and Ambassador Cutileiro, agreements on obligation to make it possible to move the population out and also to make it possible for them to return when possible.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, sir, that may very well be the case for the period of April through October of 1992. It was not a particular area that I studied in detail, because it was not necessarily applicable to what happened in my understanding in July of 1995. Again, if there are specific documents you wish to show me on that and I can comment on, I will, but I can't make a statement as to a broad number of documents I'm just not familiar with.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. We'll deal with that set of agreements. One of the agreements hasn't been admitted here. It's dated the 11th of April. But, for example, on the 22nd of May, an agreement was signed according to which the parties would make it possible for the population to be moved out in an organised manner and under police escort. The municipalities that the population would pass through would also be notified and the municipality they were being taken to would have to agree to this transfer of population. Were you aware of that agreement?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, sir, it may or may not exist, and I may have even seen it during some of my portion, but I'm not familiar with it at the moment, and I can't comment as to the details of it at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you come across any documents in which the return of refugees was prohibited, or did you come across documents that in fact provided guarantees for the return of the refugees during the entire period that we are concerned with?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: With respect to Eastern Bosnia, I don't know that I have ever come across a document, at least with respect to the military documents, which specifically says that the return of refugees into Eastern Bosnia is prohibited, in that language. Along the same vein, I don't recall ever coming across a document in that same category of material which notes that the return of Bosnian Muslim refugees into Eastern Bosnia during that period of the conflict would somehow be protected or ensured.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What you have in mind is the right to return.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. What I have in mind is a military document that specifically says that Bosnian Muslim refugees, individuals who may have been displaced prior to -- in this context prior to the establishment of the Srebrenica safe area would have some right to return in that particular context. I mean, in fact, many of the military documents that I have seen make it clear that in some particular municipalities -- there's one particularly related to Bratunac where the brigade commander is essentially saying to create ultimately the conditions so they all leave. So I can't agree with your assertion that there are military documents with respect to Eastern Bosnia that somehow can be construed to encourage or that the army supports a process to allow Bosnian Muslim refugees back into those areas during the period of the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Given that I believe that you will agree that there wasn't a military regime in place in Republika Srpska, would you agree that those issues were dealt with by the civilian authorities, and did you come across a document from the government or drafted by the president that stated that the return of refugees wouldn't be authorised? Or did you come across numerous documents, in fact, in which the return of refugees was guaranteed?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: With respect to the military document collections I'm aware of related to Eastern Bosnia, no, sir, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So you didn't come across a document prohibiting the return or guaranteeing the return of refugees. But, Mr. Butler, Eastern Bosnia wasn't the only battle-field. In the case of the entire area of Bosnia-Herzegovina, did you see any documents of mine that concerned the protection of civilians, and did you see any agreements with the other sides that concerned the guarantees issued for the return of refugees once the conditions were right for such a return, once hostilities had ceased, once the fighting had ceased?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, sir, I take your point that Eastern Bosnia is not the whole of the conflict in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Such documents may exist, but given the focus of my military analysis work, again it -- they're not relevant to what I was looking at. I may have seen them and they not registered. I don't dispute that they may exist, but with respect to the territorial area I was looking at, my answer remains the same. I did not see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you see any documents in which it said that the return of refugees was guaranteed apart from cases in which the return of refugees to Eastern Bosnia was concerned?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, sir, as I've stated prior, having not seen the documents that you're discussing or not being familiar with them, I'm not sure I can qualify what subset they're in. I have to repeat my previous answer. I'm not aware of those documents if they exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But then you would agree that if they exist at the level of Bosnia-Herzegovina, they also apply to Eastern Bosnia; right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure that I agree or disagree to anything. At this point, all I'm saying is that I'm not aware of the documents that you're referring to. Since I'm not aware of the documents that you're referring to, I have no basis by which to either agree or disagree as to what they mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Butler, would you agree that you have no basis for qualifying the act of moving the population from Eastern Bosnia, because you don't know on what basis the move was done?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The basis for -- under which the moves were done, I believe, are incorporated in the various military directives, specifically 4, directive 7, directive 7/1, as well as in other military documents which reflect how military operations in Eastern Bosnia were carried out. So that is the basis of my expertise to make these conclusions. If there are -- and I will -- you know, there may very well be, although I have not seen them, documents from the political leadership or the Supreme Command that reflects that it should not be done this way and that those orders were disobeyed by the military, but again I don't see them, I've not come across them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would just say in this series of questions leading up to the ultimate question, Mr. Karadzic put a lot of hypothetical questions about documents which were vaguely suggested it would provide some kind of legal basis for the movement of virtually the entire Muslim population out of the Cerska-Konjevic Polje, et cetera, area in 1992 and then is putting it to the witness, Well, you don't know about these documents so you have no basis to say why they have been moved out. So I think it's only fair if he's saying there is a document that he has, that exists, that would show that the movements of the population out in late 1992, early 1993, was pursuant to some legal order which has been vaguely alluded to, he should put it to the witness before saying to the witness, Well, you don't know about this document, you have no basis. Sorry for that lengthy explanation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With all due respect, Mr. Nicholls, I'm not intending to convince or convert this witness. I will yet have opportunity to convince the Trial Chamber. All I'm interested in is to find out the basis for his report. If Mr. Butler is making a report without knowing about key documents regulating the move of civilians, then some of his conclusions may be groundless. That is my point. That is the Defence case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I would like you to concentrate on more specific issues, Mr. Karadzic. Just general questions and answers do not help you or the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Excellency, but I do have to deal with 1992 and 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You said that directive 4 orders an attack on civilians. Can you show me where it says "Attack civilians"?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again with the provision that the language as translated is accurate, the line is: "While the rest of the wider forces in the Podrinje region are to exhaust the enemy, inflict the heaviest possible losses on them, and force them with the Muslim population to leave the Birac, Zepa, and Gorazde areas." Clearly in the context of a directive -- a military directive, the only way to inflict the heaviest possible losses relates to military attack. Again, I don't specifically see the phrase in there that the army is to attack civilians in the same context as they would attack a military force. However, I believe that it is absolutely implicit that in a broad sense, given the fact that one of the operational objectives here is to force out the army and the Muslim population, and the phrase here is "force them with the population to leave the area," it does make, at least in part, the civilian population an object of military attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: With all due respect, Mr. Butler, these are minor aberrations with major consequences. There is a clear distinction here between an attack and killing of the enemy and the reference to the civilian population, which is quite separate. It does not say anywhere here there would be an attack on the civilian population or that the civilian population should be expelled. That's why it is important to know that the civilian population was willing to leave, as they were willing to leave Vecici, and that their return was guaranteed. This is the Defence case, that these minor aberrations and -- which are insufficiently understood have major consequences. Where do you draw from here that civilians would be attacked? Does this text make a distinction [Realtime transcript read in error "addition continuation"] between the enemy and the civilians?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I'm late, but I'm going to object to that long argument which a question that has already been asked and answered was thrown in at the end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Correct. The simpler your question is, the better off -- the better off you will be, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Still I would like Mr. Butler to say does the mention of inflicting as great losses as possible refer to civilians or only to the enemy? But I don't want an opinion from him. I want only facts.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Again, sir, as I testified previously, the language says what it says, and also one has to look at how the actual operations were conducted by the VRS military forces on the ground. I take your point that, you know, my interpretation of the language isn't the controlling factor. It is the interpretation of your military commanders as to what the language says, what the language means, and how it was implemented that should be the controlling factor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It is not by chance that I asked you whether the warring parties have certain obligations, primarily the warring party that declared war against the civilian population. From your point of view, is it lawful and legal to seek shelter behind your own civilians, to mix your troops with civilians, and to turn your own civilian population into an army on a daily basis?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I can say is that obviously international law on armed conflict applies to all parties and that they should seek, wherever possible, to minimise civilian casualties. I can't speak in broad terms as to the lawfulness of -- or legality of military forces, as you say, potentially shielding behind a civilian population or turning a civilian population into an army on a daily basis. Those are specific situations. And where examples come forward, I can comment on them if that's what you desire, but I can't speak in more detail than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Here's the example, Mr. Butler: It is my assertion that in the sector which in that spring of 1993 -- in fact, we'll show you a map made by your own government. In the sector controlled by the Muslims in 1993 and which we had accepted would eventually belong to the Muslim federal unit, the Muslim army was mixed with civilians, civilians who, as required, put on uniforms and fought, and they were inflicting heavy losses on us. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: With respect, sir, this question is so vague that I don't know that I can answer it. I mean, what sector are you referring to specifically?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And again, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before we move on, probably I need your assistance, Mr. Nicholls. Page 40, line 22, the last part of Mr. Karadzic's earlier question which you referred to as the real question. The transcript reads like this: "Does this text" - directive 4 - "make addition continuation between the enemy and the civilians?" I take it that it should read: Does this text make distinction between the enemy and the civilians?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I think that's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before we move away, can you answer that question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. The previous question relating to the text making a distinction between the enemy and civilians, is that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Drina Corps --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I'm looking now. It says "force them with the Muslim population to leave the areas." So again if -- assuming that the language syntax is correct in the English language, I read that that the objective is not simply to force the Bosnian Muslim military forces away from the area. It takes also the fact that part of the goal is to force the Muslim military -- I'm sorry, the Muslim civilian population as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Okay. I will leave it at that. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With your leave, Your Excellency.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The question was: Is there any difference between inflicting losses on the enemy or does it stretch to inflicting losses on civilians? More precisely, are the civilians integrated into this passage about inflicting losses on the enemy?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. I believe the -- again, matter of syntax language, perhaps, but the way that it's written, inflict -- when it says the phrase "inflict the heaviest possible losses on them," I take that to be the military forces. And for -- and force them with the Muslim population to leave Birac. Now, having said that in a syntax sense, in a military sense I don't know how that you could divorce the two, particularly if you understand where the Bosnian Muslim civilian population is in those areas and where the military forces are defending them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That was not the question, Mr. Butler. I'm now beginning to wonder about your bias. Does this reference to inflicting losses apply only to the army, and is it the case that civilians are mentioned only later?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, Mr. Butler has given his answer, and it's for you to make submission later on based upon what he said. If you continue, it's just an argument.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see 1D5548 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I will now try, Mr. Butler, to put short questions that can be answered with yes or no, but you are free to expand whenever you see fit. Is this zone familiar to you?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Could we lower the picture a little so Mr. Butler can see that this is the map of Srebrenica and Cerska. Could we scroll down a little so as to see the top. No, the other way. Could you please zoom in for the witness. I believe this has been notified. Can we now see the whole picture again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this Podrinje, the area you dealt with, Mr. Butler?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the area that was the primary focus of my military analysis work. I believe it's referred to generally as the upper Podrinje area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know that in all peace plans it was envisaged and accepted by the Serbian side that this area would become part of the Muslim constituency, Muslim entity?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
